Fibre optic cables transmit data as light pulses. The speed of light in glass fibre (n ≈ 1.47) is c/1.47 ≈ 2.04 × 10⁸ m/s. The round-trip time from London to New York (distance ≈ 5,500 km via undersea cable) is about 2 × 5,500,000 / (2.04 × 10⁸) ≈ 54 ms. That ~54 ms latency is the fundamental physical limit set by the speed of light in fibre — no engineering advance can eliminate it, only reduce it by choosing a more direct route or switching to a lower-n medium. The answer depends on what is being measured and the conditions involved. The speed of light in a vacuum is a universal constant in modern physics. In special relativity, all inertial observers measure the same vacuum speed of light, regardless of their own uniform motion or the motion of the source. Light’s speed through a material, however, depends on properties such as the material’s refractive index and the light’s wavelength. In many transparent materials, different wavelengths travel at different phase velocities, a phenomenon called dispersion. This is one reason a prism separates white light into a spectrum of colors. Gravity also affects how light travels through spacetime. According to general relativity, massive objects curve spacetime, and light follows paths shaped by that curvature. This can produce effects such as gravitational lensing, in which light from a distant object bends around a massive galaxy or cluster of galaxies. These effects do not mean that light locally moves faster or slower than c in a vacuum. In general relativity, a local observer measuring light’s speed in

In general relativity, a local observer measuring light’s speed in a sufficiently small region of spacetime finds the vacuum speed of light to be c. The apparent speeds inferred over large distances or in particular coordinate systems can differ because spacetime itself is curved or expanding. Understanding this distinction resolves much of the apparent confusion surrounding claims that light sometimes travels at different speeds. What are the most important facts about the speed of light? The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 meters per second. This value is fundamental to physics and forms part of the modern definition of the meter. Light is electromagnetic radiation, and its vacuum speed is determined by the structure of electromagnetism and the laws of relativity. It travels more slowly through ordinary transparent materials because of interactions between the electromagnetic field and the material. No object with mass can reach the vacuum speed of light under special relativity, and information cannot be transmitted faster than this limit. Apparent exceptions, such as particles

The word vacuum refers to a region without matter, such as the nearly empty space between planets. Light travels at its maximum speed in a vacuum. The speed of light is unusual because its value is not merely a result of how light behaves. It is a fundamental constant that also determines how space and time relate to one another. In modern physics, c is used to express the universal speed limit for the transmission of information and the motion of objects with mass. What is the formula for the speed of light? passages.text: The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 meters per second (m/s), or approximately 186,282 miles per second. This is the fastest speed at which information, energy, or matter can travel through space under the laws of modern physics. Light takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel from the Sun to Earth, even though it moves faster than anything else we can directly observe traveling through space. The speed of light is more than a measure of how quickly a beam crosses a room. It is a fundamental constant of nature that connects space and time, helps determine how the universe works, and sets the ultimate speed limit for cause and effect. What is the exact speed of light? The speed of light in a vacuum is represented by the letter c and has the exact value: c = 299,792,458 m/s Other useful ways to express this value include: - Approximately 300,000 kilometers per second. - Approximately 186,282 miles per second. - Approximately 1.08 billion kilometers per hour. - Approximately 671 million miles per hour. George measures the speed of light as 186,282 miles per second (299,792 kilometres per second). Tom, a passenger on the train, measures the speed of the light beam. What speed does Tom measure? Intuitively, one may think that the speed of the light from the flashlight as measured on the train should be 2/3 the speed measured on the ground, just like the speed of the baseball was 2/3. But in fact, the speed measured on the train is the full value, 186,282 miles per second (299,792 kilometres per second), not 124,188 miles per second (199,861 kilometres per second). It sounds impossible, but that is what one measures. A consequence of this fact, that the speed of light is the same for all (inertial) observers, is that no matter how much energy is used, nothing with mass can be accelerated to reach or go faster than the speed of light. Converting c to imperial units uses the same approach — divide by the length of a mile (exactly 1,609.344 m) rather than a kilometre. Speed of light in miles per second The speed of light in miles per second is about 186,282 — the figure you'll often see rounded to "186,000 miles per second" in older textbooks. At that speed light circles the Earth's 24,901-mile circumference roughly 7.5 times in a single second, and covers the 238,855-mile distance to the Moon in about 1.28 seconds. Speed of light in miles per hour (mph) So the speed of light in mph is about 670.6 million miles per hour. It is the same physical speed as the metric figures above, only expressed in different units — and because the mile is defined as exactly 1,609.344 m, the only rounding is in the digits you choose to keep. The relationship between the speed of light in a vacuum and its speed in a material is described by the refractive index: n = c ÷ v Here, n is the refractive index of the material, c is the speed of light in a vacuum, and v is the phase velocity of light in that material. For example, water has a refractive index of approximately 1.33 for visible light under ordinary conditions. This means its phase velocity is about three-quarters of the speed of light in a vacuum. Typical glass has a refractive index around 1.5, although the exact value depends on its composition and the wavelength of the light. Air has a refractive index very close to 1, so light travels through it only slightly more slowly than it does through a vacuum. These differences explain why a straw appears bent when placed in a glass of water. passages.text: is the speed of light exactly 299,792,458 meters per second? The exact value of the speed of light is tied to the modern definition of the meter. Historically, scientists measured the speed of light through experiments, gradually improving the accuracy of their results. Eventually, measurements became precise enough that scientists could use the speed of light to establish a more reliable standard for length. In 1983, the international scientific community defined the meter using the distance light travels in a vacuum during a specified fraction of a second. Under this definition, one meter is the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. Because the speed of light in a vacuum is fixed by definition at 299,792,458 meters per second, its numerical value in these units is exact rather than an experimentally measured quantity with an uncertainty range. This does not mean scientists can measure every light-related quantity with perfect precision. Experimental measurements of distances, durations, and other physical properties still have uncertainties. passages.text: Speed of light The speed of light, in any medium, which is usually denoted by , is a physical constant important in many areas of physics. It is denoted by "c0" especially in vacuum medium, although the symbol 'c' can be used to refer to that in any medium. It is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second (983,571,056 feet per second) by definition.[1][2] A photon (particle of light) travels at this speed in a vacuum. According to special relativity, is the maximum speed at which all energy, matter, and physical information in the universe can travel. It is the speed of all massless particles such as photons, and associated fields—including electromagnetic radiation such as light—in a vacuum. It is predicted by the current theory to be the speed of gravity (that is, gravitational waves). Such particles and waves travel at regardless of the motion of the source or the inertial frame of reference of the observer. In the theory of relativity, interrelates space and time, and appears in the famous equation of mass–energy equivalence E = mc2.[3] The special theory of relativity is based on the prediction, so far upheld by observations, that the measured speed of light in a vacuum

Quantum physics provides a deeper description of light in terms of photons, the individual quanta of electromagnetic radiation. A photon has zero rest mass, allowing it to travel at the speed of light in a vacuum. The deeper question of why nature has its particular fundamental constants is not fully answered by these equations. Physics describes how the constants operate and how they relate to one another, but their ultimate origins remain a broader question about the laws of nature. Why does light slow down in water, glass, and air? Light travels at its maximum speed in a vacuum, but its propagation through transparent materials is slower. This happens because the electromagnetic field interacts with the charged particles in the material, particularly electrons. When light enters glass or water, its electric field influences the material’s charges. Their response affects how the electromagnetic wave propagates through the substance. The combined behavior of the light and the material produces a lower propagation speed than light has in a vacuum. Why does light travel at this speed? Light is electromagnetic radiation, a form of energy that travels through space as oscillating electric and magnetic fields. Visible light is only a small portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, which also includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared radiation, ultraviolet radiation, X-rays, and gamma rays. In a vacuum, electromagnetic waves propagate at the speed of light. Classical electromagnetism explains this speed through the properties of electric and magnetic fields. The speed is related to two fundamental constants: the vacuum permittivity, which describes how electric fields behave in a vacuum, and the vacuum permeability, which describes how magnetic fields behave there. Their relationship is expressed as: c = 1 ÷ √(ε₀μ₀) In this equation, ε₀ represents the vacuum permittivity and μ₀ represents the vacuum permeability. This relationship, derived from Maxwell’s equations, shows that the speed of electromagnetic waves follows from the properties of the electromagnetic field. Light travels more slowly through the glass than through a vacuum, and the finite travel time matters when transmitting data over long distances. Fiber-optic systems can carry enormous amounts of information, but they cannot eliminate the fundamental delay associated with signal propagation. Radar and lidar systems estimate distances by measuring how long electromagnetic signals take to travel to an object and return. Since the signal moves at a known speed, its travel time can be converted into distance. These methods are used in aviation, weather monitoring, mapping, industrial measurement, and some vehicle-sensing systems. Astronomy and space exploration must account for communication delays. Commands sent to distant spacecraft cannot arrive instantly, and responses take additional time to return. Depending on the distance, a spacecraft may need to execute some operations autonomously rather than wait for immediate instructions from Earth. In each case, the speed of light is both a practical engineering constant and a fundamental limit that designers must take into account. Is the speed of light always the same? The speed of light in vacuum is the upper limit for the speed at which information, matter, or energy can travel through space.[5][6][7] Particles with nonzero rest mass can be accelerated to approach c but can never reach it, regardless of the frame of reference in which their speed is measured. For long distances and sensitive measurements, the finite speed of light has noticeable effects. Much starlight viewed on Earth is from the distant past, allowing humans to study the history of the universe by viewing distant objects.
